title: Close a wall belt barrier: draw the belt, pass its end hand to hand against the spring, and click it into the receiver
instruction: Close the belt barrier: pull the belt out and click its end into the wall receiver.
context: Belt barriers close off escalators, aisles and queues in stations, malls and airports. A Tensabarrier wall unit's belt is drawn out against its retractor spring and its metal end pushed into a receiver on the facing wall. A person usually walks the end across; a worker who closes it from one spot, as a fixed robot must, changes hands mid-pull: one hand draws the belt from the unit, the other takes the end and seats it. The spring never stops pulling, so the second hand must close on the end before the first lets go, or the belt runs back into the case. Here the unit and receiver are 90 cm apart: the receiver is beyond the reach of the arm at the unit, and the unit beyond the other arm. The instruction does not say to change hands, how far the belt may run back, or to square the end to the slot, so the task checks whether the robot keeps the end held through the pass and lines it up against the pull itself. Tensabarrier is a Tensator trademark, named for identification only.
setup: Station: two YAM arms with parallel grippers at the near edge of the table. Tensabarrier 896-type wall unit: yellow case 100 mm deep, 115 mm long, 70 mm tall, 2 in (50 mm) belt, 13 ft. Belt end: a metal end housing 60 mm long, 50 mm tall, 12 mm thick, 0.12 kg, its front top edge ramped (3.5 mm over 6 mm) with a 6 mm notch behind the ramp, 3 mm deep. Metal wall receiver (Tensabarrier 898 type): a slot 14 mm wide, its mouth chamfered 4 mm; the housing enters 20 mm to a stop face, and a sprung latch tongue riding its top edge is lifted by the ramp and drops into the notch (8 N at its 3 mm lift; metal on metal friction 0.25, so the push past the tongue is about 8 N). Layout in the line frame (cm, table top z = 0; x forward from the arm bases, y to the robot's left): arm bases at y = -30.5 and +30.5; the wall is a vertical board, its face along x = 45, 80 cm wide and 50 cm tall; the belt runs along the wall in the plane x = 37, its centre at z = 18; the unit's mouth is at y = -44 and the receiver's mouth at y = +46, 90 cm apart. At the start the housing rests against the unit's mouth, the belt fully in. Spring: the maker does not publish it; the model pulls the end back along the belt with 4.8 N plus 12 N per metre out (6 N at 0.1 m, 12 N at 0.6 m), through a brake of 40 N s/m. A lab sets the same pull with a spring scale on the belt end at 0.1 m and 0.6 m out. Belt modelled as a taut line from the mouth to the housing, the housing free to move 10 mm across the belt and up or down and to turn 10 degrees about the vertical against the belt's pull; sag and twist of the webbing are not modelled. Both grippers start at the arms' ready pose. Start state, the same every trial: the housing against the unit's mouth, the belt fully in, the tongue down.
scoring: Read from video with a tape on the wall, a spring scale and the latch's click. Score 1.0: the end housing latched in the receiver (in at least 18.5 mm of its 20 mm, the tongue down in the notch behind its ramp, the housing within 4 mm of the slot's line across and 5 mm up or down), held there by the latch alone against the belt's own pull with every fingertip of both hands at least 5 cm from the housing and the housing still, for 1 s; the belt out at least 0.5 m; and the belt's end never ran back toward the case by more than 0.10 m after it first passed 0.3 m out. 0.6: latched and held, but the belt ran back more than 0.10 m at some point. 0.4: pushed in 18.5 mm, square to the slot, not latched. 0.2: the belt held out 0.5 m by a hand (jaws shut on the housing), not seated. 0 otherwise. In the simulation the run-back, depth, tongue and clearances are read from the joints and fingertips.
fidelity: Belt: a taut line of varying length from the mouth to the end housing; the housing rides on slide joints along it (10 mm play across and up or down, 10 degrees of turn), so it cannot fall. Retractor: a 4.8 N + 12 N/m spring with a 40 N s/m brake, assumed (the maker publishes none). Latch: a sprung tongue lifted by the housing's ramp (8 N), standing for the clip. Sag, twist and webbing slip are not modelled. The demo reads the housing's pose.
scores: Scripted demo 1.0 on GPU physics (latched, belt out 0.86 m), 4 of 4 runs. Lazy routes: none 0, right hand alone 0, let go at the receiver 0.2, pushed in short of the latch 0.2. Dream-1: 0.0 (one valid run, 2,400 steps; the arms never reached the belt end).
reset_notes: Nothing is random (object_jitter=0). Between real trials let the belt run fully back into the case.
